newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE-Taiwan's futures bourse to take on rivals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Taiwan's futures bourse to take on rivals.

text.p: Does the early bird always catch the worm?
Not necessarily, says the head of Taiwan's fledgling futures exchange, who hopes the exchange will outpace established rivals in Chicago and Singapore despite their head starts.
"The government has set October for the start of the futures exchange," said Richard Chen, director of the Taiwan International Mercantile Exchange Corp, the island's first futures market.
"Things are proceeding on our original schedule," Chen told Reuters in a recent interview.

Chen nevertheless was reluctant to give his full commitment to that timetable, saying he could not rule out the possibility that the market, which has suffered a series of delays, might have to wait another "month or two".
Chen's office began operations in March soon after parliament adopted a long-delayed Futures Trading Law that cleared the way to open the exchange.
PRESSURE MOUNTS TO LAUNCH EXCHANGE
Chen said the government was anxious to see Taiwan's own futures exchange up and running and that time was running out.
"Why are we in such a hurry? We don't have the luxury to wait," he said.
Chen was referring to the January 9 launch of futures pegged to Taiwan's stocks by the Singapore International Monetary Exchange and Chicago Mercantile Exchange.

The CME and SIMEX kicked off the Taiwan stock-index futures contracts over the fierce objections of Taiwan regulators, who had pleaded in vain for them to wait until Taipei could open its own futures market and launch its own stock-index contracts.
Pressured by acute demand and its own pledge to liberalise Taiwan's financial markets, Taipei on August 1 finally lifted a ban on local trading of the CME and SIMEX contracts.
The SIMEX contract has fared better before and since the ban was lifted, with daily volume averaging 1,000-2,000 lots while the CME contract often trades less than 100 lots.
SIMEX A CONTENDER, CME AN ALSO-RAN
Chen described the CME contract as a "failure", but said the SIMEX was becoming a threat to his own planned contracts.
"If we wait longer, will we find a very strange situation in which all local players will go to Singapore and trade the Taiwan stock-index futures in the SIMEX?"
"We have to be very aggressive," he said.

Chen said the Taiwan exchange would have a clear competitive edge over the offshore competitors, since it will be the only market offering futures trading linked directly to Taiwan's main index, the Taiwan Stock Exchange's proprietary TAIEX.
The CME futures are based on Dow Jones & Co's Taiwan Index, while the SIMEX uses Morgan Stanley's Taiwan Index. Both claim a close correlation to the TAIEX.
INVESTORS EAGER TO PLAY AT FUTURES

Chen said Taiwan investors were eager to learn and join in what he called the "sophisticated game" of futures trading, but said the CME was not likely to provide the new Taiwan exchange with much competition.
"We can feel a lot of local brokerages are ready to embrace Taiwan stock-index futures trading. We can feel the market's zeal and anticipation," he said.
"Investors are very eager to participate, but as far as I know not many are interested to trade in the CME."
A language barrier and time difference were both keeping Taiwan retail customers away from the Chicago market, and probably vice-versa, he said.
"I don't think people living in Chicago will be interested in the Taiwan stock-index futures. They must be crazy if they do. The Taiwan market is just too far away," Chen said.
The SIMEX has a better chance of wooing Taiwan retail business, due to its proximity as well as Singapore's widespread use of the Mandarin Chinese dialect that is standard in Taiwan.
But the SIMEX does not maintain the kind of close contacts with the Taiwan stock market that Taiwan investors would expect, Chen said.
TAIWAN MARKET IS TAIWAN'S TO LOSE
"It's difficult for a foreign exchange to compete with a local exchange unless we screw up first," Chen said. "No one else knows our market better than ourselves."
The door for cooperation with major foreign futures exchanges remained open, he added.

Chen said Taiwan, where futures have been traditionally regarded as high-risk financial instruments all but indistinguishable from gambling, has a lot of catching up to do, but voiced confidence that the local futures market had significant potential.
A main task for the island's financial regulators would be to educate investors on how to hedge their investment risks through derivatives trading, he said.

"Once Taiwan's stock investors figure out they can have so much fun during the process of trading derivatives...they will become much more sophisticated investors and we will have booming financial markets," Chen said.
"I have every reason to be optimistic," he said.
